title: Steamed Pork Ribs with Black Bean
subtitle: dim sum ribs with fermented black bean, garlic and chilli
excerpt: Small pieces of pork rib marinated in fermented black beans, garlic, chilli and cornflour, then steamed until tender and juicy. A classic dim sum dish ready in about 50 minutes including marinating time. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Steamed spare ribs with black bean sauce (pai gwut in Cantonese) are one of the most ordered dishes on dim sum trolleys across Guangdong, Hong Kong and Cantonese restaurants worldwide. The dish is documented in Cantonese cookbooks from the mid-twentieth century and has remained largely unchanged: the combination of fermented black beans, garlic and cornflour to tenderise and coat the ribs is a fixed formula. At home, a bamboo steamer over a wok produces the closest result to the dim sum version.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the ribs for up to 4 hours in the fridge. Steam straight from the cold marinade, adding 2 to 3 minutes extra to the cooking time.

glossaryTerms.definition: Small black soy beans that have been salted and fermented until intensely savoury and slightly funky. They are sold dried or in jars. Rinse before using to reduce saltiness and roughly chop or crush to release their flavour.

A Cantonese tradition of small dishes served alongside tea, typically eaten for breakfast or lunch. The word means 'touch the heart'. Classic dim sum includes dumplings, steamed ribs, sticky rice in lotus leaf, turnip cake and custard tarts.
A Chinese rice wine with a nutty, amber flavour used widely in marinades, sauces and braises. Named after the city of Shaoxing in Zhejiang province. Dry sherry is the closest substitute.

Finely milled maize starch used to thicken sauces and coat ingredients before frying. In steamed rib marinades it absorbs moisture and tenderises the meat, giving the ribs a smooth, velvety surface after cooking.

content.text: This classic
dim sum
dish takes about 50 minutes and serves 4 as part of a spread. Pork ribs are chopped small, marinated in
fermented black beans
, garlic, chilli,
Shaoxing wine
and
cornflour
, then steamed until tender and glossy.

Ask the butcher to cut the ribs into 3 to 4 cm pieces through the bone with a cleaver. This is not easy to do with a standard kitchen knife. Small pieces are essential, both for cooking evenly in a steamer and for eating without cutlery.
What you need

items.prepNote: chopped into 3-4 cm pieces through the bone

content.text: Method
Rinse the rib pieces under cold water and pat dry. This removes any bone dust from the cutting.

Combine the fermented black beans, garlic, ginger, Shaoxing wine, soy sauce, oyster sauce, cornflour, sugar, sesame oil and chilli oil in a bowl. Add the ribs and mix well to coat. Leave to marinate for 20 minutes at room temperature.
Spread the ribs in a single layer in a heatproof shallow dish or bamboo steamer lined with parchment.
Set up a steamer over a wok of boiling water. Place the ribs in the steamer, cover tightly and steam for 25 to 30 minutes until the pork is cooked through and tender.
Check the water level halfway through and add boiling water from a kettle if needed.
Scatter with spring onions and serve directly in the steaming dish with steamed rice or as part of a dim sum spread.

items.symptom: Ribs are still tough after 30 minutes
items.cause: Steam level dropped because the water ran low, or the lid was not sealed.
items.fix: Check the water level at 15 minutes and top up with boiling water. Use a tight-fitting lid or cover tightly with foil.

items.cause: Fermented black beans and oyster sauce together can be very salty, especially if the beans were not rinsed.
items.fix: Always rinse the black beans thoroughly before using and omit the soy sauce if the marinade smells very salty.

items.cause: Too much cornflour or the dish was not in a single layer during steaming.
items.fix: Spread the ribs in a single layer and use no more than 1.5 tbsp of cornflour. The coating should be light and smooth, not thick.

content.text: Where this dish lives

Steamed spare ribs with black bean are one of the most recognisable dim sum dishes, served in bamboo baskets alongside siu mai, har gow and turnip cake in Cantonese yum cha restaurants throughout the world. The home version is straightforward: the same marinade, a wok with a steamer insert, and patience. Eaten this way as a main dish over rice rather than as one small piece from a trolley, the flavours are generous and satisfying.
